title: SIEM
summary: A Security Information and Event Management platform is a centralised system that ingests logs and telemetry from across an estate, normalises them into a common schema, correlates events over time, and evaluates detection rules to raise alerts that a security operations centre can triage. In practice a SIEM is three coupled capabilities: collection and parsing, a searchable hot and warm store with a query language, and a rules and correlation engine with alerting, case management and reporting on top. Its value depends far less on the vendor than on data quality and coverage. A rule is only as good as the fields it can rely on, so normalisation decisions, timestamp handling, and reliable identity resolution across endpoints, identity providers, cloud control planes and network sensors determine whether detections are precise or noisy. Detection engineers therefore treat the SIEM as a product with a content pipeline: they map log sources to what MITRE ATT&CK techniques they can observe, write and version rules, measure precision and recall against known-good and known-bad telemetry, and retire content that only produces fatigue. Common failure modes are predictable. Ingesting everything without enrichment produces volume without context; ignoring time zone and clock skew breaks correlation windows; broad rules with single-event triggers flood analysts; and quiet log sources create blind spots that adversaries exploit precisely because nobody alerted. Effective operators tune the platform deliberately, using allow-lists with expiry dates, entity risk scoring rather than raw severity, and periodic purple-team validation to prove that a technique which should be detected actually is.
objectives: You will be able to explain how a SIEM pipeline collects, parses, normalises and stores telemetry, and identify where parsing errors silently break downstream detections.
You will be able to assess log source coverage against MITRE ATT&CK techniques and state honestly which techniques your estate cannot currently observe.
You will be able to write and tune correlation rules that use entity context, thresholds and time windows rather than single-event triggers.
You will be able to diagnose false-positive floods by tracing an alert back through normalisation, enrichment and rule logic to its root cause.
You will be able to design retention and hot/warm/cold tiering that balances investigation needs, cost and compliance obligations.
You will be able to validate detection content with controlled test telemetry and record the evidence that a rule fires when it should.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-92, Guide to Computer Security Log Management
NIST SP 800-61, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

beginner.definition: A SIEM is a Security Information and Event Management platform. It is one central system that collects logs from across your whole estate. It cleans them into a common shape, stores them, and checks them against detection rules. When a rule matches, the SIEM raises an alert for analysts to review.
beginner.whyItMatters: Logs live in hundreds of places: laptops, servers, cloud accounts and network devices. Without one central system, nobody can see the whole picture. A SIEM is what lets you connect a strange login on one system to a strange file change on another. It is also where your detection rules actually run.
howItWorks: Agents and connectors on your systems forward their logs to the SIEM.
A parser reads each log format and breaks it into named fields, such as user and host.
Normalisation then renames those fields so every source uses the same field names.
The events land in a searchable store, and older data moves to cheaper storage.
Detection rules run against the incoming events and raise an alert on a match.
Alerts go to a queue with case notes, so an analyst can investigate and record a decision.
beginner.example: Imagine a large building where every room keeps its own notebook of who came and went. If something is stolen, you would have to walk to every room and read every notebook. A SIEM is the front desk that collects all those notebooks each night and keeps them in one place. Rules act like a careful clerk who reads them all and shouts when something looks wrong.
takeaways: A SIEM is only as good as the logs you feed it.
Bad log parsing silently breaks the rules that depend on those fields.
Know which log sources you are missing; those are your blind spots.

exercises.title: SIEM - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: SIEM - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: SIEM - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.title: SIEM - EXTREMELY HARD
exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.
